There is a comfortable story about AI and access to justice. Roughly 92% of the substantial civil legal problems of low-income Americans get no or inadequate legal help. 1 Lawyers are scarce and expensive. AI is abundant and nearly free. Therefore AI closes the gap.

Every step in that argument is defensible. The conclusion still does not follow, and we now have enough evidence to say why.

The evidence assembled here points somewhere more uncomfortable than either the optimistic or the pessimistic version of this debate. It is not that AI produces bad legal information â increasingly it does not. It is that legal information is not the only, and may not be the binding, constraint once a litigant enters the system. The controlled interventions we found that supply information have increased procedural participation without producing detectable improvements in case outcomes. And representation â the intervention everyone assumes works â turns out to work conditionally, in ways suggesting that lawyers are not primarily delivering legal knowledge either.

Meanwhile, two studies of federal court records document the same pattern since generative AI became widely available: substantially more self-represented filing, without evidence of improved litigation outcomes. 23 , 24

## Methodology

How these sources were selected. We ran a structured â not a formal systematic-review-protocol â search across peer-reviewed journals, working-paper repositories, research-institution reports, court administrative data, and government statistics, for evidence meeting three criteria: (1) it measures an outcome, not a sentiment; (2) where it makes a causal claim, it uses a design capable of supporting one, or the source itself disclaims causal identification; (3) it is a primary source, or a faithful report of one that we traced back to the original.

We separate findings into four evidence tiers, marked throughout: primary source (government data, administrative records, original survey instruments), peer-reviewed research , working paper or preprint (not yet peer-reviewed), and program or advocacy report (typically no control group).

One further convention, which matters most in Parts 4 and 5: claims that go beyond what a cited study states are marked as interpretation. Everything else is a report of a source's own finding. Where we draw an inference the underlying authors did not draw, we say so and say why â and where an inference is one of several readings the data supports, we give the alternatives.

Two exclusions are worth stating. We excluded vendor benchmarks and vendor-published performance claims entirely; they appear nowhere in what follows. And we excluded program evaluations reporting only volume served, satisfaction, or forms filed. Not because those programs are unserious â because they do not answer the question. That exclusion removed a substantial majority of the published material we encountered.

Every figure in this article was verified against the primary document, in its current version, in August 2026. Where a working paper has been revised, we cite the current revision and say so. Where a widely circulated figure could not be traced to a primary source, we say that rather than repeating it â six such figures appear in Part 1. Where we quote from a published abstract rather than from body text, the source entry says so.

## The funnel: what "improving access to justice" could mean

Almost every disagreement in this field is a disagreement about which stage of a funnel is being measured. Setting the funnel out first makes the rest of the evidence legible.

Problem â Recognition â Information â Action â Participation â Legal position â Disposition â Real-world outcome â Welfare

- Problem. A civil justice situation occurs.

- Recognition. The person identifies it as something the legal system addresses.

- Information. They learn what rules apply and what options exist.

- Action. They file, answer, or otherwise engage.

- Participation. They appear, respond to motions, meet deadlines.

- Legal position. They have a defense, a claim, or a bargaining chip that carries weight.

- Disposition. The case ends in a judgment, dismissal, or settlement.

- Real-world outcome. They keep the housing, avoid the garnishment, obtain the status.

- Welfare. They are better off, accounting for costs and any market response.

Representation, self-help materials, and AI are not stages â they are interventions that enter the funnel at different points and can only affect stages downstream of where they enter.

The funnel is an analytical decomposition, not a claim that every case passes through these stages in sequence. Information can produce recognition; a lawyer can produce both; leverage can determine a disposition before any hearing occurs. The stages are a vocabulary for asking what was measured , not a model of how cases proceed.

### What "outcome" means in this article

The word does most of the work in this literature and is used for at least four different things. We distinguish them throughout:

- Procedural outcome â an answer filed, an appearance made, a deadline met. Stages 4â5.

- Legal outcome â a judgment, dismissal, settlement, possession order, or monetary recovery. Stage 7, also called a disposition .

- Real-world outcome â housing retained, garnishment avoided, status obtained. Stage 8.

- Welfare outcome â the real-world result net of costs, and of any market or institutional response. Stage 9.

Where a source says "outcome" without specifying, we say which of these it measured.

The pattern this article documents is that most claims about AI and access to justice are supported at stages 2 through 5, while the evidence that matters sits at stages 7 through 9. Movement at an early stage does not propagate automatically to a later one.

## Part 1: The gap is real, and it is not shaped the way most people think

The headline number is sound. The Legal Services Corporation's 2022 Justice Gap study â a NORC AmeriSpeak probability-panel survey fielded 18 October to 4 December 2022, covering 2,003 adults at or below 125% of the federal poverty line plus 3,305 above it, alongside a four-week census of requests for help across LSC-funded organizations â found that low-income Americans get no or inadequate legal help for 92% of their substantial civil legal problems. LSC-funded organizations turn away 49% of eligible requests due to limited resources. 1 (Primary source. There is no 2025 or 2026 edition.)

Two more recent findings complicate the standard framing.

The gap is not confined to poverty. The State Bar of California's 2024 Justice Gap Study â over 6,000 respondents, fielded 8 August to 7 October 2024, published 2025 â found that between 72% and 75% of households in every income group experienced at least one civil legal problem, and that between 84% and 86% of civil legal problems in every income group received no or inadequate help. 2 (Primary source.) The income bands run from at-or-below 200% of the federal poverty line to above 120% of area median income. On the narrower substantial-impact measure the spread is wider and non-monotonic â 79%, 76%, 73%, 78% â which still supports the point.

One comparison to avoid, and we flag it because it is tempting: California's 85% is not comparable to LSC's 92%. LSC's figure covers substantial-impact problems; California's comparable substantial-impact figure is 77% . The 85% covers all civil legal problems. These are California figures, not national ones.

A legal right to counsel does not produce counsel. New York City has a statutory right to counsel in eviction proceedings. The NYC Comptroller's May 2025 report found the share of eligible tenants receiving full representation fell from 71% in the fourth quarter of FY2021 to 42% in the fourth quarter of FY2024 , with a monthly low of 30% in March 2025 ; in the Bronx, from 81% to 31% over the same quarters. 3 (Primary source â government oversight report.)

The methodology deserves a note, because it cuts both ways. The Comptroller counts only cases with two or more appearances, which excludes the fastest-disposed cases where representation is lowest. But it also marks an entire case as represented if counsel appeared at any single appearance. Both choices inflate the figure. True representation across all filed cases is plausibly lower than 42%.

Capacity, not entitlement, is the operative constraint.

### Six numbers you will see cited that do not survive checking

This field has an unusually severe zombie-statistic problem. Anyone writing about it should know which numbers are contaminated â and in four of these six cases, the problem is worse than the standard correction suggests.

There's a comfortable assumption running through most corporate AI strategy right now: a skilled person plus an AI tool will outperform either one alone. It's intuitive, it's reassuring, and it lets organizations roll out AI everywhere without asking hard questions about where, specifically, it helps.

It's also not what the evidence shows.

We identified eight controlled empirical studies â through a structured literature search described below, not an arbitrary shortlist â that compare at least two of unassisted human performance, AI-alone performance, and human-plus-AI performance on a well-defined task, using real accuracy, speed, or quality measurements rather than survey sentiment. Only a subset of the eight contain all three conditions in a single design; the remainder provide controlled two-arm evidence (most often human-alone vs. human+AI, or human-alone vs. AI-alone) that helps test whether the broader pattern generalizes across tasks â which study includes which conditions is noted in each section below and in the summary table. They span clinical diagnosis, management consulting, customer support, professional writing, and software engineering. These are not eight versions of the same experiment. They differ in design, sample, and what they measure: most are randomized controlled trials, one is a staggered field rollout with a randomized pilot; some measure a single 20-minute task, one follows real production work across three companies over months. Read individually, each study answers a narrow question about its own task and population. Read together, a pattern emerges that is not "AI helps." It's closer to a fault line: AI's advantage is real, large, and reproducible on some tasks, and reverses into a disadvantage â or simply disappears â on others that look, to a human, more or less the same. A large independent meta-analysis of the broader literature finds a closely aligned pattern, which is the strongest evidence this isn't an artifact of which eight studies we happened to pick.

## Methodology: how these eight studies were selected

To avoid presenting a hand-picked set as more authoritative than it is, we ran a structured â not a formal systematic-review-protocol â literature search across Google Scholar, Semantic Scholar, PubMed, SSRN, NBER, arXiv, the ACM Digital Library, and IEEE Xplore for controlled studies published in 2022 or later that met all of the following: (1) compare at least two of unassisted human performance, AI-alone performance, and human+AI performance; (2) use a real or realistic work task, not a survey or self-reported opinion; (3) report a quantitative outcome â accuracy, speed, a graded quality score, or an error/completion rate, not satisfaction; (4) are peer-reviewed and published, or are a working paper from an established research institution or lab, not a vendor blog post or marketing study; and (5) cover clinical diagnosis, knowledge work, customer service, writing, or software engineering, with a broader scan across education, forecasting, hiring, translation, legal work, and classic human-AI "centaur" research to check for major work we might otherwise miss. This is a transparent, criteria-driven search, not a formal systematic review â it does not follow a pre-registered PRISMA-style protocol, log exact search strings or per-database result counts, or use a second independent screener, and readers who need that standard of evidence should treat it accordingly.

That search surfaced roughly two dozen candidates. Most were excluded for a specific, checkable reason: some measured self-reported time allocation or satisfaction rather than task performance (a large Microsoft 365 Copilot field study of over 7,000 workers, NBER Working Paper 33795, measured how workers reallocated their time, not whether their output improved); some were observational rather than randomized, which weakens causal claims (a study of 72,000+ GitHub pull requests found AI-assisted PRs merged faster, but without random assignment); and a few strong two-arm studies (AI-alone vs. human-alone, no combined condition) in medicine and forecasting were kept as corroborating context rather than counted as primary sources, to avoid overweighting any single domain. The eight studies below are the ones that survived that screen with the strongest designs available â eight primary studies in total, including one earlier preprint (Peng et al., 2023) that we retained specifically as a labeled historical predecessor to a later, stronger study on the same question, rather than as independent evidence in its own right.

We also checked our pattern against the closest thing to independent confirmation available: Vaccaro, Almaatouq, and Malone's 2024 meta-analysis in Nature Human Behaviour , which pooled 106 prior experiments (370 effect sizes) comparing human-alone, AI-alone, and human-AI teams across many task types. 1 Its headline finding â that human-AI combinations underperform the better of either alone on average, with the effect reversing between decision-making tasks (where combining hurts) and content-creation tasks (where combining helps) â is a closely aligned, task-dependent, non-uniform pattern to the one this piece finds in its own eight studies. That convergence is meaningful: it means the "it depends on the task" conclusion below isn't a quirk of which eight studies we selected, but matches what a systematic review of the wider literature already shows.

## The clearest three-way test: doctors, AI, and doctors using AI

The most direct answer to "who does better work" comes from a single-blind randomized clinical trial published in JAMA Network Open on October 28, 2024, run across Stanford, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, and the University of Virginia. 2 Fifty US-licensed physicians (26 attendings, 24 residents; median 3 years in practice) in family medicine, internal medicine, and emergency medicine were randomized into two groups and given up to six clinical vignettes â patient histories, exam findings, lab results, adapted from a landmark 1994 diagnostic-systems study â to work through in a one-hour session. One group used conventional resources only (UpToDate, Google, and similar). The other used those same conventional resources plus ChatGPT Plus (GPT-4). A third, non-randomized condition ran the same vignettes through GPT-4 alone, three separate times, with no physician involved. Participants completed 244 cases in total (125 in the LLM group, 119 in the control group).

The results, as published 2 :

On the clinical cases tested, the LLM working alone scored a median of 92% â clearly ahead of both physician groups, including physicians who had access to the LLM. Adding ChatGPT to a physician's workflow did not produce a statistically significant accuracy gain over conventional resources alone. Physicians using AI were modestly faster on average (519 seconds per case vs. 565), a difference the paper's own results text reports as not statistically significant (95% CI â195 to 31 seconds, p=0.20).

It's worth being precise about what this study does and doesn't show, because the authors themselves are unusually direct about it. Their own words: "Results of this study should not be interpreted to indicate that LLMs should be used for diagnosis autonomously without physician oversight." The clinical vignettes were curated and summarized by human clinicians rather than experienced firsthand, the study excluded patient interviewing and data collection, and the setting was acontextual â none of which capture the full scope of real clinical reasoning. What the study does show, within that bounded scope, is that a physician's real-time judgment about when to trust or override an AI's suggestion did not reliably improve on the AI's unaided output â and on these cases, the human addition did not clear the bar of statistical significance in either direction.

A second, larger trial by an overlapping author team complicates this picture in an important way. A follow-up randomized controlled trial published in Nature Medicine in 2025 â led by several of the same researchers, using a different task design â found that physicians using GPT-4 on patient care tasks did score significantly higher than physicians using conventional resources alone: +6.5 points (95% CI 2.7â10.2, p<0.001). 3 In that trial, 92 physicians were split across three arms (conventional resources, GPT-4 plus conventional resources, and GPT-4 alone), and â as in the first study â GPT-4 alone was statistically indistinguishable from physicians using GPT-4 (difference â0.9%, 95% CI â9.0 to 7.2, p=0.8). GPT-4-assisted physicians also took meaningfully longer per case (+119 seconds, p=0.02).

Put the two studies from the same research group side by side and the honest conclusion isn't "human+AI helps" or "human+AI doesn't help" â it's that the answer depends on task design in ways not yet fully understood, even to the researchers running near-identical experiments. Across both studies, GPT-4 alone was not significantly worse than the physician+GPT-4 condition; however, the studies differed materially in whether physician+AI improved on physicians using conventional resources â a significant gain in the 2025 trial, no significant gain in the 2024 trial.

## Where "human + AI" earns its keep â and where it stops

The diagnosis studies aren't outliers so much as one end of a spectrum visible across the research base. The clearest articulation of why comes from a large field experiment run by researchers at Harvard Business School with Boston Consulting Group, since published in Organization Science as "Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier." 4 The paper's central idea â the "jagged frontier" â is that AI's competence doesn't fall off gradually as tasks get harder, the way a human's does. It's extraordinary on some tasks and unreliable on adjacent ones that look, to the person assigning the work, about the same.

In that study, 758 BCG consultants completed 18 realistic consulting tasks, some with GPT-4 access and some without. On tasks the researchers classified as inside the model's competence zone, AI-assisted consultants completed 12.2% more tasks , 25.1% faster , at measurably higher quality than the unassisted group. On a task designed to sit outside that zone, AI-assisted consultants were 19% less likely to produce a correct solution than the unassisted control group â a statistically significant effect (p<0.01).

The finding that should complicate any tidy "just train people better" narrative: consultants who additionally received explicit training in how to prompt and collaborate with the model did not do better on the out-of-frontier task â they did worse . The trained group's correctness dropped by about 24.5 percentage points relative to control, compared to a 13.9-point drop for consultants using GPT-4 without training (both significant; the gap between the two AI conditions was marginally significant, pâ0.08â0.10). Training did modestly improve output quality on inside-frontier tasks. But on the one task built to sit beyond the model's competence, teaching people to use the tool more fluently made them more confidently wrong, not less.

That's the uncomfortable version of the "jagged frontier" finding: the fix for AI failing outside its competence zone isn't more prompting skill. It's knowing, task by task, whether you're inside the zone at all â something the paper doesn't show people learn to detect just by getting better at using the tool.

## The real, repeatable win: AI narrows the gap between your best and worst performers

One of the most consistent effects in this body of research is this: AI's largest gains tend to go to less experienced workers, not the strongest ones.
